Empirical Research Plan: “Does International Trade Cause Faster Economic Growth?”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Cross-sectional Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) following the spirit of Frankel & Romer (1999).

Why IV?  
• The treatment (trade openness) is endogenous: faster-growing economies may trade more, and trade policy is chosen partly in response to growth prospects.  
• Geography (distance, being land-locked, common language, etc.) is predetermined and plausibly exogenous to contemporary policy choices.  
• Geographic characteristics generate strong first-stage power because they enter the canonical gravity equation for bilateral trade flows.  
Alternative methods (DiD, RDD) are not feasible because we lack well-timed shocks and a running variable. A pure cross-section OLS comparison would be biased.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i  ≡  Trade openness of country i = (Exports_i + Imports_i) / GDP_i in the late-20th-century benchmark year (e.g., 1990 or average 1985-1995).

Instrument (Z_i)  
Predicted trade share from a gravity model that uses only exogenous geographic variables:  
1. Bilateral log distance between i and j  
2. Indicator for whether i or j is land-locked  
3. Common land border, common language, colony links (all predetermined)  
4. Country j’s population and area (size controls)  

Predicted bilateral flows Ť_ij are summed over all partners j and divided by GDP_i to obtain Z_i.

Control group / Counterfactual  
There is no discrete “control” country: identification comes from cross-country variation in Z_i. Countries with low predicted trade (e.g., land-locked in the interior of Africa or Central Asia) serve as counterfactuals to coastal, well-connected economies.

Timing  
Single benchmark period. (If panel data are later added, we can construct a Bartik-style interaction instrument, but the baseline is strictly cross-sectional.)

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance (Cov[Z_i, T_i] ≠ 0).  
Plausible: gravity variables are among the strongest predictors of actual trade volumes.

A2. Exclusion (Z_i affects growth only through contemporaneous trade).  
Potential concern: geography can influence growth via disease environment, factor endowments, or transportation costs for domestic commerce. Mitigation: control for absolute latitude, land area, malarial ecology, and continent fixed effects; show robustness to excluding tropical and land-locked observations; use over-identification tests with multiple instruments.

A3. Independence / As-Good-As-Random (Geography is predetermined with respect to modern growth shocks).  
Reasonable: continental drift long precedes modern economic outcomes.

A4. Monotonicity (countries with “better” geography never trade less because of that geography).  
Gravity theory implies monotonicity in distance and adjacency; exceptions are unlikely.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country spillovers in the first stage beyond trade).  
Some spillovers exist (one country’s location influences another’s trade route), but first-stage is constructed at the bilateral level and summed; these spillovers are already embedded in the instrument.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Geography affects growth directly (violates Exclusion).  
Remedy:  
• Include controls for climate (absolute latitude, mean temperature), natural resource rents, soil quality, malaria ecology index.  
• Conduct Oster-style bounded-effects test; look at coefficient stability when adding controls.

Threat 2: Weak instrument in subsets of the data (small island economies, oil exporters).  
Remedy:  
• Report first-stage F-statistic (rule-of-thumb ≥ 10).  
• Use LIML and Anderson-Rubin tests as robustness.  
• Show results excluding potential weak clusters (islands, OPEC).

Threat 3: Measurement error in trade or GDP.  
Remedy:  
• Average trade and GDP over a 5-year window to smooth noise.  
• Use Penn World Tables and World Development Indicators separately; compare.  
• Demonstrate robustness to deflators and PPP vs market exchange rates.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
# ----------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)    # fast 2SLS
library(AER)       # ivreg for overid tests
library(sandwich)  # robust vcov
library(lmtest)    # coeftest

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ----------------------------------------------------------
trade <- read_csv("country_trade_growth.csv")   # contains exp, imp, GDP, growth
gravity <- read_csv("bilateral_gravity.csv")    # bilateral distances etc.

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct variables
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Treatment: trade share
trade <- trade %>% 
  mutate(trade_share = (exports + imports) / gdp,
         ln_gdppc    = log(gdp_per_capita),
         growth      = (ln_gdppc - lag(ln_gdppc, n = 1))/years_between)

# Instrument: predicted trade share from gravity
gravity <- gravity %>%
  mutate(pred_trade = exp(-1 * log(distance_km)) * 
                      border * language * colony)   # illustrative

predicted <- gravity %>%
  group_by(exporter) %>%
  summarise(pred_trade_share = sum(pred_trade, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  rename(iso = exporter)

data <- trade %>%
  left_join(predicted, by = "iso") %>%
  mutate(lat_abs = abs(latitude)) %>%
  drop_na(trade_share, pred_trade_share, growth)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Baseline IV regression
# ----------------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- growth ~ trade_share + lat_abs + log(population) + continent |
                       pred_trade_share + lat_abs + log(population) + continent

iv_res <- feols(iv_formula, data = data, se = "hetero")   # robust SEs

summary(iv_res, cluster = "continent")

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Over-identification + weak-IV diagnostics
# ----------------------------------------------------------
# (a) Hansen J if multiple instruments)
ivreg_res <- ivreg(growth ~ trade_share + lat_abs | 
                   pred_trade_share + lat_abs, data = data)
summary(ivreg_res, diagnostics = TRUE)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: drop land-locked + tropical (<23.5°)
# ----------------------------------------------------------
rob_data <- data %>% filter(landlocked == 0, lat_abs > 23.5)
rob_res  <- feols(iv_formula, data = rob_data, se = "hetero")
etable(list(Main = iv_res, Robust = rob_res), keep = "trade_share")
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Heckscher-Ohlin, endogenous growth with technology diffusion) predicts a positive effect. Prior literature finds an elasticity around 0.2.  
Expectation: A 1-percentage-point increase in Trade/GDP raises long-run annual growth by roughly 0.02–0.04 pp (i.e., a country whose trade share is 50 pp higher grows ≈1–2 pp faster per year).

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion from growth except via trade ………………… 0.5 (plausible but arguable)  
C3: Independence / as-good-as-random geography ………… 1  
C4: Monotonicity (better geography → weakly ↑ trade) …… 1  
C5: Correct functional form & no effect heterogeneity that violates LATE … 0.5  

Total ≈ 4/5. The main caveat is the possible direct channel from geography to growth; extensive robustness and controls are therefore essential.

------------------------------------------------------------
This plan yields a transparent, testable estimate of the causal impact of international trade on economic growth while clearly acknowledging and addressing the key threats to identification.
